title: Charge Point Operator
overview: A web application for managing EV charging stations, giving operators real-time access to station health, maintenance scheduling, and third-party integrations.
description: Charge Point Operator is the internal console operators use to run a network of EV charging stations. It covers live station status, user access control, maintenance workflows, and invoicing — all built as a component-driven React application talking to a REST backend.
features: Live station management dashboard with status, uptime, and maintenance flags
Role-based user access module for operators and field technicians
Invoicing workflows tied to charging sessions
Third-party integration hooks for payment and telemetry providers
responsibilities: Developed multiple frontend modules including station management, user access, and invoicing
Implemented CRUD operations with efficient state management using Redux
Wrote unit and UI test cases using Jest and React Testing Library for better reliability
Followed component-based architecture for a scalable UI and enforced code quality through reviews

challenges.challenge: Station status needed to feel real-time without hammering the API
challenges.solution: Centralized polling with Redux-managed cache invalidation, so only stale station records refetch instead of the whole list

challenges.challenge: Invoicing screens had deeply nested, reusable form logic
challenges.solution: Extracted shared form primitives and validation into composable components, cutting duplicated logic across invoicing flows

architecture.frontend: React with a component-based, feature-folder architecture
architecture.stateManagement: Redux for shared/cross-module state, local state for isolated UI
architecture.styling: Tailwind CSS utility classes with Material UI for complex form controls
architecture.testing: Jest + React Testing Library covering critical CRUD and invoicing flows
architecture.notes: REST APIs consumed through a typed service layer to keep components decoupled from fetch logic

title: Co-Workspace Management
tagline: Operator and member portals for co-working spaces
overview: A web application for managing co-working spaces, enabling workspace operations, resource allocation, bookings, invoicing, and tenant management through dedicated operator and member portals.
description: Co-Workspace Management is a dual-portal platform: operators run day-to-day workspace operations across locations, while members book rooms, manage their workspace, and track invoices — all from a unified, state-driven React/Next.js frontend.
features: Operator dashboard with calendar, location, and tenant management
Multi-location resource and room booking system
Member portal with booking timeline and workspace management
Order processing, invoicing, and customer service ticketing
responsibilities: Developed multiple frontend modules for operator and member portals, including dashboard, calendar, location management, tenant management, order processing, invoicing, and customer service tickets
Built booking and resource management features to efficiently handle workspace reservations, room allocation, and resource availability across multiple locations
Developed member portal functionality including workspace management, booking timeline, and member details
Integrated REST APIs, implemented CRUD operations, and managed application state efficiently using Zustand

challenges.challenge: Booking availability had to stay consistent across multiple locations and overlapping time slots
challenges.solution: Modeled availability as a normalized Zustand store keyed by location/resource, so conflicting bookings are caught client-side before hitting the API

challenges.challenge: Operator and member portals shared data but needed very different UI density
challenges.solution: Split shared domain logic into hooks/services and kept presentation layers separate per portal, avoiding a bloated one-size-fits-all component set

architecture.frontend: Next.js App Router with feature-based module boundaries for operator vs member portals
architecture.stateManagement: Zustand for booking/resource state, colocated hooks for portal-specific logic
architecture.styling: Tailwind CSS with a shared design system of Material UI components
architecture.testing: Component-level checks on booking and invoicing edge cases
architecture.notes: Calendar and timeline views built as reusable primitives shared between both portals

title: Smart City
tagline: IoT device management and analytics for infrastructure operators
overview: A serverless, cloud-hosted platform that gives infrastructure operators a single place to manage IoT devices, watch sensor data come in on a live map, and set up rules that react to it automatically.
description: Smart City is the operator-facing platform behind a city's IoT device fleet — device provisioning and health, map-based sensor visualization, webhook-driven data ingestion, and a rule engine that turns raw sensor readings into alerts and automated actions. I joined after the first version had already shipped and spent a large part of my time modernizing a codebase that had fallen behind, alongside building out several of its core modules.
features: Device management for provisioning, monitoring, and tracking the health of connected IoT hardware
Map-based visualization of live and historical sensor data across managed sites
Webhook ingestion with ETL workflows that normalize incoming sensor payloads before they're stored
A rule engine for threshold-based alerts and automated actions triggered by sensor data
Per-app workspaces so operators can scope devices, rules, and dashboards to a given deployment
responsibilities: Migrated a legacy class-component codebase to functional components with hooks, module by module, without breaking the dashboards still running on the old pattern
Modernized the dependency tree to run on current Node.js LTS and fixed the compatibility breaks that surfaced along the way
Built out the rule engine, device management, app management, and analytics modules
Added map- and chart-based visualizations for sensor analytics, including device locations, historical readings, and alert states
Raised test coverage and cleaned up patterns left over from the legacy codebase, improving both readability and runtime performance

challenges.challenge: The class-to-functional migration touched shared state that dozens of existing components still depended on — rewriting it in one pass risked breaking dashboards operators were actively using.
challenges.solution: Migrated module by module behind the existing prop and context contracts, converting lifecycle methods to their hook equivalents one component at a time, and only removed the old patterns once every consumer was verified against the new implementation.

challenges.challenge: With hundreds of devices reporting on independent intervals, re-rendering the map on every incoming sensor reading made it noticeably laggy.
challenges.solution: Decoupled marker updates from the raw data stream — readings are batched and a marker only re-renders when its value crosses a rule threshold or moves out of its last-rendered bucket, instead of on every tick.

architecture.frontend: React, migrated from class components to functional components with hooks during my time on the project
architecture.stateManagement: Redux for device, rule, and analytics state shared across modules
architecture.styling: Tailwind CSS with chart and map components wrapped as reusable primitives
architecture.testing: Jest coverage added incrementally during the migration, focused on the rule engine and data-transform logic
architecture.notes: Backend runs as serverless functions (AWS Lambda) triggered by device webhooks; an ETL step normalizes each device type's payload into a canonical sensor-reading format before it reaches the rule engine

title: SIMS — Smart Inventory Management System
tagline: Multi-tenant inventory management with role-scoped access
overview: A multi-tenant inventory platform where each tenant manages their own stock, orders, and users — with low-stock alerts, full order CRUD, and four roles (Super Admin, Admin, Manager, User) that are scoped per tenant, not just per account.
description: SIMS is built for businesses managing inventory across multiple tenants from one platform. Each tenant gets its own inventory, order history, users, and alert thresholds, and every role — from Super Admin down to a regular User — is scoped to the tenant it belongs to, so nothing from one tenant is ever visible to another.
features: Multi-tenant inventory tracking, fully isolated per tenant
Configurable low-stock thresholds that trigger alerts before items run out
Full CRUD for purchase and sales orders
Four-tier role hierarchy — Super Admin, Admin, Manager, User — scoped per tenant
Notification system surfacing stock alerts and order events to the relevant roles
responsibilities: Built the multi-tenant data access layer so inventory, orders, and users stayed isolated per tenant at both the API and UI layer
Implemented configurable stock-threshold alerting, including per-tenant thresholds and alert delivery
Built CRUD flows for purchase and sales orders, including status transitions like fulfillment and cancellation
Implemented role-based UI and route guarding across four roles, each scoped to its tenant rather than global
Built the notification module surfacing threshold and order events to the roles responsible for acting on them

challenges.challenge: Roles weren't just role-based, they were role-scoped-per-tenant — a Manager in one tenant needed the same permissions as a Manager in another, but neither should see or affect the other's data.
challenges.solution: Modeled permissions as (tenant, role) pairs instead of a flat role enum, and enforced tenant scoping at the API query layer as well as route guards, rather than relying on the frontend alone to hide unauthorized data.

challenges.challenge: Threshold alerts fired on every stock update near the limit, which meant a slow-moving item hovering around its threshold could spam the same alert repeatedly.
challenges.solution: Added hysteresis to the alert logic: an alert fires once when stock crosses below the threshold and clears once stock is restocked past a buffer above it, rather than re-evaluating and re-alerting on every update.

architecture.frontend: React with role-aware route guards shared across a common component layer
architecture.stateManagement: Redux for tenant, role, and inventory state; local state for order forms
architecture.styling: Tailwind CSS with Material UI for inventory and order data grids
architecture.testing: Jest coverage on threshold-alert logic and tenant/role permission edge cases
architecture.notes: Every API call is scoped by tenant ID resolved from the authenticated session, enforced on both client and server

title: Afterwords
tagline: Confidential legacy-messaging platform (name changed for confidentiality)
overview: A platform for recording messages to the people you love and having them delivered later — right after you're gone, or years from now on a specific date. Renamed here since the real project name is under NDA.
description: Afterwords lets a user record text, audio, or video messages for the people in their life and control exactly when those messages get delivered. A network of Notifiers confirms when the user has passed, Trustees handle messages tied to future events rather than death, and Recipients simply receive what was left for them — all built around four distinct roles (Owner, Recipient, Trustee, Notifier) and five core modules: Dashboard, Messages, Notifiers, Trustees, and Profile.
features: Four role-scoped portals — Owner, Recipient, Trustee, Notifier — each seeing only what their role needs
Message composer supporting text and in-platform audio/video recording, with per-message recipient and delivery-timing rules
Multi-notifier confirmation flow: a life event is only confirmed once enough independent notifiers corroborate it
Trustee-managed delivery for event-specific messages (e.g. a future birthday) kept separate from the death-confirmation path
Chunked, resumable upload pipeline for large in-platform video recordings
responsibilities: Built the Dashboard, Messages, Notifiers, Trustees, and Profile modules end-to-end
Implemented the multi-notifier confirmation workflow that gates message delivery on corroborated confirmation rather than a single report
Built the message composer, including in-platform video/audio recording and delivery-timing configuration
Designed and implemented the trustee-managed, event-specific delivery flow as a path separate from death confirmation
Owned the video upload pipeline end-to-end, including the performance rework below

challenges.challenge: In-platform video messages could run into the gigabytes, and the first working version uploaded straight to S3 as a single request — a 1.8GB recording took 12-15 minutes to upload, long enough that users would back out or lose the recording on a flaky connection.
challenges.solution: Rebuilt the upload path around S3 multipart upload: the recording is split into fixed-size chunks in a Web Worker so encoding doesn't block the UI, chunks move through a bounded upload queue backed by a small worker pool instead of one request at a time, each chunk retries independently on failure, and the parts are batched into S3's complete-multipart-upload call once everything succeeds. The same 1.8GB file went from 12-15 minutes to 90-100 seconds.

challenges.challenge: The death-confirmation flow is the most sensitive part of the product — it can't act on a single false report, but it also can't be so strict that a real event goes unconfirmed.
challenges.solution: Modeled confirmation as a quorum: each notifier's report is logged independently, and message delivery only unlocks once a configurable number of notifiers corroborate the same event, with trustees notified at each stage so there's a human check before anything is sent.

architecture.frontend: Next.js with role-scoped portals (Owner, Recipient, Trustee, Notifier) sharing a common module shell
architecture.stateManagement: Zustand for session/role state, plus a dedicated upload-queue store tracking chunk status per in-progress video
architecture.testing: Focused test coverage on the notifier-quorum logic and chunked-upload retry paths, given how costly a bug in either would be
architecture.notes: Video capture built on the MediaRecorder API; uploads go through a Web Worker pool driving chunked, concurrent, resumable transfers into S3 multipart upload
